messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Interior Designer
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 57

He is sixty-seven now, a widowed man from Oceania who has spent most of his life arranging other people’s spaces into something calm, balanced, and livable. As an interior designer, he still notices light first when he enters a room—where it falls, what it hides, whether there is a clear line to the door. He says this as if it is professional habit, but over time it becomes clear that it is not only that. He scans every space he enters. He sits where he can see exits. He dislikes closed offices, heavy curtains, and rooms without windows. If a door clicks shut behind him, his shoulders rise before he can stop them.

The worst thing that happened to him began years ago during a work trip to a coastal development project in a remote area. He had gone to consult on a hotel renovation, expecting long site meetings, samples spread across tables, and arguments about color, budget, and humidity-resistant materials. Instead, while traveling between towns, he was taken by armed men along with two others. Even now, when he tells it, the details come in fragments rather than sequence: the smell of diesel, rough hands at the back of his neck, the hood over his face, the pressure in his bladder from not being allowed to use a toilet, the ache in his shoulders from being tied.

He is held for days in a cramped room, though he cannot say exactly how many. Time dissolves there. He learns to measure it by sounds—the scrape of a food tray, the changing heat in the walls, distant voices, once the cry of a rooster that seems impossibly ordinary. He does not know when he will be hurt and when he will be left alone, and that uncertainty becomes its own kind of torture. He tries to stay alive by designing rooms in his head. He imagines floor plans from memory, rearranges furniture, chooses fabrics for clients he may never see again. He focuses on proportions and color pairings to keep panic from swallowing him. At other moments he thinks only of his wife and whether she knows he is alive.

When he is finally released, he returns physically thinner and outwardly composed. People tell him how fortunate he is. He says the right things. He goes back to work too quickly, insisting on normality. For a while he manages by keeping busy. He throws himself into projects, spends hours obsessing over cabinetry finishes and corridor width, and accepts too many jobs because silence feels dangerous. But captivity follows him home in ways he does not anticipate. At night he wakes drenched in sweat, disoriented, clawing at the bedsheets as if his hands are tied. In the first months after his return, his wife learns not to touch him suddenly in sleep. Once, when she gently shakes his shoulder, he jerks away so violently that they both end up frightened and ashamed.

He starts avoiding anything that reminds him of confinement. He takes stairs instead of elevators, even when his knees protest. He cancels site visits to basements and storage areas, asking junior staff to handle them. During client meetings, if someone closes the conference-room door for privacy, he finds a reason to reopen it. He becomes irritable in traffic and cannot tolerate road detours. The loss of control feels immediate, not symbolic. If a contractor is late, if a delivery does not arrive, if a plan changes without warning, his chest tightens and his thoughts begin racing toward danger.

His wife dies some years later after a medical illness, and her death seems to strip away one of the last places where he had felt anchored. Since then, the nights are worse. There is no one in the house to wake him from the dreams or reassure him afterward. He often falls asleep in an armchair with the television on because a bedroom feels too enclosed and too quiet. He keeps lights on in the hallway and checks locks repeatedly, though he knows the neighborhood is safe. He hates admitting how much fear governs the shape of his evenings.

In the studio, younger colleagues know him as gifted, exacting, and difficult to surprise. They do not see how often he loses the thread of a conversation when a sound in the corridor catches him, or how he drifts for a few seconds into the old room when a client casually mentions being “stuck” somewhere. He is embarrassed by his own reactions. He tells himself he should be over it by now, that he survived, that other people have endured worse. Yet his body does not accept these arguments. In crowded restaurants he feels trapped. In windowless hotel rooms he cannot breathe. When travel is required for work, he packs meticulously, studies maps, and still considers canceling until the last minute.

He speaks about captivity with restraint, but his life is organized around not feeling it again. He maintains beauty for a living—texture, openness, harmony—while privately fighting a constant expectation that the world can narrow without warning into a locked room, a covered face, and waiting without end.
